title: Shivanasamudra Lights Bangalore
subtitle: When the Kaveri Learned to Carry Light
figure: K. Seshadri Iyer and Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV
region: Shivanasamudra Falls, Kolar Gold Fields, Bangalore and Mysore State
moral: Science serves society when power is carried beyond the waterfall.

sources.citation: Mysore Electricity Department annual reports after 1902
sources.note: Administrative record for the Shivanasamudra hydroelectric scheme.

sources.citation: Imperial Gazetteer of India: Mysore and Coorg (1908)
sources.note: Contemporary reference to Mysore's hydroelectric development.

sources.citation: M. Visvesvaraya, Memoirs of My Working Life (Government of Mysore, 1951)
sources.note: Engineer-statesman's recollections of modern Mysore works.

panels.shot: sweeping low-angle wide of Shivanasamudra falls with faint transmission lines stretching toward a distant city

dialogue.text: In Mysore’s twilight of princes and steam, K. Seshadri Iyer and a boy-king dared to ask: can the rage of the Kaveri carry light to far-off mines and a sleeping city?

panels.shot: wide establishing shot of Mysore countryside with distant palace and British cantonment

dialogue.text: The year is 1898. Mysore is called a ‘model state’ by British officials, yet its nights glow only with oil lamps and its wealth lies hidden in deep, dark rock.

panels.shot: underground cross-section view, slightly low-angle, of miners in Kolar Gold Fields

dialogue.text: At Kolar Gold Fields, British companies hunger for more ore, more speed, more profit. The mines need power—vast, steady, cheap. Steam engines gulp coal; the costs choke the venture.

panels.shot: intimate interior mid-shot in the Mysore durbar hall, slight low-angle on Seshadri Iyer addressing the regency council with the young prince present

dialogue.text: Under Dewan Seshadri Iyer, the regency rules for the minor Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV. The Dewan sees in Kolar’s hunger a chance to remake Mysore with a new kind of power.

panels.shot: medium close-up on Seshadri Iyer presenting a map, with the young prince in profile

dialogue.speaker: K. Seshadri Iyer & Young Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV
dialogue.text: “We will make the Kaveri climb hills and cross plains as light.”

panels.shot: wide shot at Shivanasamudra, slightly high-angle, showing surveyors at work

dialogue.text: They choose Shivanasamudra, where the Kaveri breaks into furious falls. Here, gravity itself can drive great turbines. But no one in India has yet sent such power so far.

panels.shot: interior workshop mid-shot, with engineers poring over blueprints and alternator designs

dialogue.text: Alternating current is still new, argued over in Europe and America. Mysore’s officials weigh risks: can fragile wires carry this invisible force sixty, seventy miles without failing?

panels.shot: small council-room shot, mid-level, Dewan in debate with a British official while the young prince listens quietly

dialogue.text: Mysore will bear the cost; the company will buy the power. Imperial gazetteers later note this quiet bargain: a princely state funding modern works, not merely paying tribute.

panels.shot: dramatic wide shot of construction at Shivanasamudra, with scaffolding and masonry in the spray of the falls

dialogue.text: Through the late 1890s, stone by stone, coil by coil, the powerhouse rises. Turbines from abroad meet local craft; Mysore’s own lines department grows around this roaring classroom.

panels.shot: interior of the completed powerhouse, wide shot, with massive generators and engineers in place

dialogue.text: By 1902, the scheme stands ready. Government reports will soon record a new phrase in Mysore’s ledgers: ‘Shivanasamudra hydroelectric station, supplying Kolar Gold Fields.’

panels.shot: symbolic close-up of Seshadri Iyer’s hand on a control lever, with the prince watching in the background

dialogue.speaker: K. Seshadri Iyer & Young Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV
dialogue.text: “From this fall, may all Mysore be lit.”

panels.shot: dynamic wide shot showing the turbines beginning to spin and lights flickering on in the station

dialogue.text: The switch falls. Water drives steel; steel drives copper. Invisible currents hum into the long lines that run over hills and dry tank-beds toward the buried gold.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye following transmission lines across countryside toward Kolar

dialogue.text: Across sixty miles, the lines carry alternating current at high voltage—among Asia’s earliest such journeys of power from river to distant industry.

panels.shot: interior wide shot of a KGF surface workshed as electric motors start up

dialogue.text: At Kolar, motors turn without steam boilers, cages rise with new speed, and the deep levels glow brighter. The mine books show it plainly: costs fall, output climbs.

panels.shot: soft-lit interior of the Mysore palace study, mid-shot of the now slightly older prince reading a report with Seshadri Iyer nearby

dialogue.text: Dewan Seshadri Iyer does not live to see every fruit of this work, yet the young king grows into his role with these reports as his early scriptures of governance.

panels.shot: wide shot of Bangalore’s South Parade (MG Road area) at dusk, with the young Maharaja and officials inspecting new street lamp posts

dialogue.text: From Shivanasamudra, spare capacity and new lines now reach Bangalore. Mysore’s capital prepares to trade its smoky lamps for arcs of electric brightness along its main roads.

panels.shot: dramatic low-angle wide of the first electric street lamps flaring to life over Bangalore’s street

dialogue.text: When the current is released, a rush of light runs down the line. Bangalore’s streets blaze with a new, steady glare—reportedly among the earliest electric street lighting in Asia.

panels.shot: gentle mid-shot of the Maharaja looking up at the lights, with a portrait of Seshadri Iyer in the background

dialogue.speaker: K. Seshadri Iyer & Young Krishnaraja Wodeyar IV
dialogue.text: “Power must not end at the mine; it must reach the citizen.”

panels.shot: time-lapse style wide shot of Mysore State maps and later works, dissolving from falls to gridlines

dialogue.text: From this first cascade of wires grew Mysore’s wider grid, the later dams of Visvesvaraya’s age, and a new idea of rule: that a state’s glory lies in how far it carries light.
